# [TASK] movie-service: support a year-range filter on discover

## Task
Support a year-range filter (`yearFrom`/`yearTo`) on movie-service's
discover endpoint, alongside the existing exact-year filter.

## Scope
`TmdbClient` → `MovieService` → `MovieController`'s discover path only. The
TMDB-shaped facade (`TmdbFacadeController`) stays exact-year-only —
confirmed unaffected by both review passes, including a direct check that
its own `@RequestParam` list and HTTP contract are untouched.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] `GET /api/v1/movies/discover` accepts optional `yearFrom`/`yearTo` query params alongside the existing `year`
- [x] When both are given, results map to TMDB discover's `primary_release_date.gte`/`primary_release_date.lte` params — verified at the real HTTP-request layer via WireMock query-param matchers, not just mocked-argument assertions
- [x] When only the existing single `year` is given, current exact-match behavior is unchanged — regression-tested at the unit and WireMock layers, including an explicit assertion that the new range params are *absent* from the outgoing request
- [x] Giving both `year` and a range together is rejected with a clear validation error (`ValidationException` → 400 `ProblemDetail`) rather than silently picking one — tested at both the service and HTTP layers, both OR-branches (`year`+`yearFrom` and `year`+`yearTo` independently)
- [x] Unit + WireMock integration tests cover: range-only, exact-year-only (regression), and the conflicting-params validation error

## Estimate
**Hours:** 5

## Notes
`TmdbClient.discoverMovies` gained `yearFrom`/`yearTo`, mapped to TMDB's `primary_release_date.gte`/`.lte`. `MovieService` rejects conflicting year filters and anchors a bare year to Jan 1 / Dec 31. Both `@Cacheable` keys were widened to include the new params — otherwise a range query and an exact-year query collide on the same cached page.

Deliberately not done here: no `yearFrom <= yearTo` ordering check (a reversed range just returns nothing), and `discoverMoviesRaw` has no validation guard of its own — safe today only because its other caller passes null/null.
